title: The old harper
hook: an old musician, abandoned by his audience, plays for God alone in a graveyard (Masnavi 1.1913ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heraclitus, and Marcus's own line that nature loves change. Your line was change is natural. What changed around you yesterday, and how did you meet it? Day one hundred eighty-nine.

The wedding singer everybody once wanted. The athlete twenty years after the last game. Anyone who was once very good at something, and then the calls stopped. Applause is a kind of food, and when it goes, the hunger can be hard to admit. Yesterday Marcus told us change is natural. Today Rumi tells a story about what someone does after that kind of change, when the crowd has gone home for good. It's the first of three days with one character. Today: the old harper.
screen: `WHEN THE CALLS STOP.` → `APPLAUSE IS A KIND OF FOOD.` → `THE OLD HARPER.`

segments.voice: The story is in Book One of the Masnavi, Rumi's long poem of stories. In the days of Umar, the second caliph after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, there lived a harper in Medina. Rumi says his voice was so lovely it made nightingales lose their senses, and one breath of his song could make a gathering feel alive. Then he grew old. His voice cracked. His hands got stiff. Rumi describes the voice that once charmed hearts as now so harsh that nobody wanted it. The invitations stopped. He had no money, and he had nothing else he knew how to do. So one day he took his harp and walked out of the city to the graveyard. And there, among the graves, where no one could hear, he played. Rumi has him say something like this: all my life you gave me breath, and I spent it on others. Now I'll play for you, God, and you'll have to be my patron, because no one else will pay. He played and wept until he fell asleep with his head on a grave, the harp as his pillow. Notice what's happened. He's playing badly, alone, for an audience he can't see. For the first time in his life, the playing isn't for applause. The song has nowhere to go but upward. Some readers hear themselves in him: everything we do for someone to notice, and the strange freedom of doing one thing for no one at all. What happens next is tomorrow. For now, stay with him in the graveyard, playing. Your line: play for no one.
screen: `A SINGER WHO MADE NIGHTINGALES FAINT.` · `OLD, CRACKED, FORGOTTEN.` · `HE PLAYS AMONG THE GRAVES.` · then, large: `PLAY FOR NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with no audience. For now, just sit. Nobody is watching, nobody is scoring this, and nothing will be posted. Breathe, and notice if part of you still wants to do it well for someone. Let that part rest. Later today, pick one small thing, a song in the car, a drawing, tidying a drawer, and do it for no one. The bell holds the time.
Umar. The second caliph after the Prophet Muhammad, who in Rumi's story is sent by a dream to a graveyard. Today's word.
Your line: play for no one. Today, do one small thing well that nobody will ever see, and don't tell anyone about it. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of the Masnavi often read its stories slowly, a section at a time, and in Sufi circles this story is told as a picture of doing good work for God alone, not for praise.

fork.setup: you're the harper. your voice is gone, the invitations have stopped, and you have no money. what do you do?
options: keep knocking on doors, hoping for one more wedding.
take your harp to the graveyard and play for God alone.
sell the harp and never play again.
fork.reveal: he walks out to the graveyard and plays among the graves, for God, until he falls asleep on his harp.

original.note: Persian: the harp, the old musician's instrument in Rumi's story. the Persian story is called the tale of the old harper.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about an old man who lost his voice.
what it means: when the audience is gone, the playing becomes for God alone.
what a scholar hears: Rumi's old harper, a Sufi picture of ikhlas, sincerity: doing a thing for God and not for the watching crowd.
